extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of literature; creative writing students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, analyzing, and composing first-person unreliable narrators: detecting textual clues to a narrator's bias and psychology, and using narrative techniques (background, repetition, symbolic perception, stream-of-consciousness) to make a narrator manifestly unreliable or psychologically revealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of third-party or factual corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator offers highly-colored perceptions and interpretations given without any third-party or factual corroboration to demonstrate these as accurate, or even to suggest awareness of personal bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: 'I would not be attempting to offer my audience objective facts of a recognizable reality, but rather my highly-colored perceptions and interpretations, given without any third-party or factual corroboration to demonstrate these as accurate, or even to suggest my awareness of my personal bias.' An effective unreliable narration foregrounds this absence of objective verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective first-person perspective vs omniscient narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the classic omniscient (all-knowing) third-person narrator, the first-person unreliable narrator does not offer mutually agreed-upon objectivity and instead gives his/her own view of what happened and why it matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page wording: 'the first-person unreliable narrator never suggests they are like the God of their world by offering you a mutually agreed upon objectivity... but rather gives you his/her own view.' Use first-person limitations to create unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration as revelation of narrator psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's version of events and character descriptions build to reveal his/her personal prejudices, anxieties, fears, tastes, delusions, and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: 'an unreliable narrator’s version of events and characters in the story will also build to reveal, simultaneously, his/her own personal prejudices, anxieties, fears, tastes, delusions, and even beliefs.' Make narrative content double as psychological portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions imply family and cultural shaping
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative descriptions often imply the family and cultural environments that shaped the narrator's views and contributed to how they perceive and make meaning from the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page: 'The descriptions will often also imply the family and cultural environments that shaped his/her views, and so contributed to how he/she perceives and makes meaning from the world around them.' Use culturally specific imagery and background cues to explain biased perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide narrator background and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should give background on who the narrator is, where they grew up or lived, and why the particular event compels them to tell the story, so readers can infer why the narrator sees the world that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice from the page: 'To achieve this you might make the narrator give background on who they are, where they’ve grown up or lived, and why the particular event they are recounting has compelled them to tell the story.' Background grounds unreliable perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition, exaggeration, patterns of thought, and symbolic perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Place noticeable repetitions, exaggerations, patterned thoughts, and especially symbolic perceptions into the narrator's voice to make the story as much about the narrator’s psychology as about plot events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page quote: 'By way of placing into the mouth of your narrator noticeable repetitions, exaggerations, patterns of thought, and especially symbolic perceptions, your story... would become as much about the narrator’s psychology as it is about the events he/she is unfolding.' These stylistic devices signal unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection of personal issues onto others
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator projects their own personal history or relationships onto other characters or the audience, treating these projections as objective reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from opening: narrator projects issues with his father onto the audience: 'I’ve revealed some issues regarding my relationship with my father; and even more, I’ve projected these onto you as if they were the objective truth.' Projection is a marker of unreliable perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readerly strategy: detect clues and infer hidden psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should listen for clues, markers, repetitions, and ironic distance to act like an 'arm-chair therapist,' inferring why the narrator perceives and describes things as they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page: 'a reader... might begin to take on the role of an arm-chair therapist, listening for clues and markers in the narration that signal why the narrative voice perceives and describes things the way they do.' Encourage active, interpretive reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask why the narrator is telling the story (narrative motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always ask WHY a person is telling his/her/their story — motive for telling is a key criterion for evaluating narrator reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced in related resources: the 'What is Point of View?' video 'insists that we should always ask WHY a person is telling us his/her/their story.' Motive analysis helps reveal bias, omission, or self-justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness as a technique for unreliable voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream-of-consciousness attempts to record the ebb and flow of thoughts, feelings, impulses, memories, and perceptions/interpretations, and is a mode that often deepens first-person unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page: 'Stream-of-Consciousness ... attempts to get down on paper the ebb and flow of thoughts, feeling, impulses, memories, and perceptions/interpretations that go on in each of our minds.' Use this technique to expose unfiltered, conflicting perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic distance and close reading to reveal unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Close reading can expose an ironic distance between what the narrator believes and what the text implies; perceptive readers can draw conclusions the narrator does not recognize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from 'Araby': readers observe religiously shaped imagery and sexual impulse conflict and gain 'ironic distance' to see the narrator's misreadings. Teaching guidance: use textual detail to show where perception departs from probable reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative perception becomes narrative reality (distinguish from objective reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: In unreliable narration, the narrator's perceptions become the reality of the narration even when they are likely far from the external or objective reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page phrasing: 'My perceptions of you would now become the reality of the narration of my story, but they are most likely far from the reality of how you are looking at me now on your screen.' Highlight the difference between narrated reality and external facts.
